chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Sindi from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Isma'il ibn al-Subbah who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the tailor to whom goods are entrusted; if he damages them or loses them, is he liable for compensation? He said, 'Yes, compensate him for what his hands have earned (caused), for indeed you gave him to repair, not to ruin.'

key_terms.اَلْقَصَّارُ: The tailor (specifically one who cleans/presses woolen garments), used here as an example of a worker.
key_terms.مَا جَنَتْ يَدَاهُ: What his hands have earned/caused (idiom for direct action or negligence).
key_terms.يُسَلَّمُ إِلَيْهِ: Is entrusted to him / is handed over to him.
key_terms.يُغَرَّمُهُ: Is he made liable for compensation / is he fined.

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on compensating a worker for damaging or losing entrusted goods?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to clarify the scope of liability in *ujrah* (employment) contracts, distinguishing between mere custody and active work. The Imam emphasizes that compensation is strictly limited to the value of the damage caused by the worker's own actions ('what his hands earned'), reinforcing the Shia legal principle that liability is tied to fault rather than absolute guarantee. This hadith serves as a foundational text for commercial jurisprudence, ensuring fairness by preventing excessive penalties for entrusted goods.
